author: yellowstone times
title: Montana State University schedules fifth annual Climate Week focusing on local impacts
text:
Montana State University will host its fifth annual Climate Week from November 17 to 20 on the Bozeman campus. The event is organized by MSU students and faculty and will focus on the effects of climate change in the local community, as well as possible solutions. All events are open to the public at no cost.
Bode Kostick, a senior studying environmental science and one of the organizers, said, “Climate change is significantly threatening Bozeman and the Gallatin Valley and will continue to get worse in the future. Climate Week is aimed at promoting conversations around climate change in these especially uncertain times. The goal is to equip students and our community with the tools to promote social and political change.”
The week begins on Monday with a session on writing public comments at the MSU Library from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m., followed by a student film showcase about climate and environmental issues at 5:30 p.m. in Procrastinator Theater. Students will introduce their films and lead discussions afterward.
On Tuesday, an Electric Vehicle Showcase will take place from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. north of the Strand Union Building, where attendees can learn about electric vehicles directly from owners.
Wednesday’s schedule includes “After-WARD: A Panel on the Future of Bozeman’s Water Needs” from 5–7 p.m. in Romney Hall, Room 306, featuring city staff, WARD proposal organizers, and local developers discussing water management amid changing climate conditions. Also that evening, Climbing for Climate offers participants an opportunity to use climbing walls at the Student Wellness Center while learning how outdoor activities can motivate climate action.
Gracie Caldwell, an environmental science junior and president of Campus Climate Coalition at MSU, said, “I’ve been involved in Climate Week since freshman year. We’re really trying to pave the way for students to not just participate in events and climate action-based activities but to become climate leaders in their respective career fields.”
Thursday’s events include a Baucus Climate Scholars Panel from 12:10 to 1:30 p.m., featuring students and alumni sharing their work with organizations such as Disney and The Nature Conservancy.
That evening Karin Kirk will give a talk titled “NASA Edited Climate Change Out of My Work. What Would You Do?” from 6 to 8 p.m., describing her experience as a former NASA science writer whose references to climate change were removed after the 2024 election.
Paul Lachapelle, professor of political science and member of MSU’s faculty-led Climate Solutions Group, stated: “Faculty are beyond excited to be partnering again with these motivated students who are showing their leadership qualities to provide outstanding learning opportunities on what many scientists consider to be the most consequential issue facing humanity.”
The week’s activities are sponsored by Campus Climate Coalition and Climate Solutions Group at Montana State University.
More details about schedules can be found at https://www.montana.edu/communitydevelopment/climateweek.html.
